doc.title: Joe Segal — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Dizzy's 1947 band with Chano Pozo on 52nd Street
summary: He saw Dizzy's big band in a tiny 52nd Street room and discusses Afro-Cuban jazz and the street's scene.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Playing with and understanding Thelonious Monk

blocks.x: So going back to Dizzy. Did you ever encounter his band? Was it ’47 with Chano Pozo and that?
I saw them on 52nd Street, yeah.

They were in a place that was so small; it was like a cracker box. I mean, I don’t think there was six inches between the space of the ceiling and the top of the trumpeter’s heads. They had to go up first and then the trombones and then the saxes, and they had to leave in reverse. That way. It was so small. Yeah, Chano. And Dave Burns in the trumpet section...
Him I didn’t know. I’m not sure, could have been. Al McKibbon on bass, and Ken Gates on piano. Who was it? Maybe Joe Harris on drums.
Ok. What was your impression, because I mean they were, you know, exploring and pushing the envelope here.
I loved it. I loved all that big band stuff.
And the Afro-Cuban now entry into big band and bebop since there.
Yeah, well Cubana Be Cubana Bop and all that, and Manteca.

There’s a wonderful story where Al McKibbon talks about Manteca, how it came about, and he kind of does it in the voice of Chano Pozo, and it’s really quite cute there. But you know there was - it was a collective effort there. Because Chano had the idea, and then Dizzy and - was it Gil Fuller - then kind of put the finishing touches on it. Just to be there and experience that, cause this is new territory, forging new territory that hadn’t necessarily been part of the jazz landscape there.
How was it received? I mean were people/audiences excited? Did they embrace it?

Oh yeah, the street was just burgeoning. Everyplace was packed, you know. You could hear Eddie Condon’s guys on one side and hear bebop. You could hear Billie Holiday or Eckstine, Errol Garner, everybody, you know. Art Tatum, go nuts!
